topIssues.title: Archive node snapshots contain a gap in historical data
topIssues.author: JB273
topIssues.body:
Hi team,

We are using the snapshot from https://datadirs.optimism.io/ and it appears to be so that the provided snapshot here holds a gap for historical data.
We use the RPC mainly on The Graph indexing and we see the same missing data there (which is obvious), we have consulted with another indexer/RPC provider and they see the same issue.
It looks that the server from where the snapshot was created was in a pruning state (or was before)!

A couple of questions, can you confirm (and test);

1. If the snapshot should hold the complete historical data (from the bedrock block obviously)
2. Check if the data is available for the request attached from the snapshots provided by datadirs.optimism.io

We tested with this below curl request:
```
curl -sS "$RPC" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "jsonrpc":"2.0",
    "method":"eth_call",
    "params":[
      {
        "to":"0x4200000000000000000000000000000000000006",
        "data":"0x18160ddd"
      },
      {
        "blockHash":"0x093a99185048338f9a43a0877d3d9d7b012aa2bc7007f632b3690758b778f49d"
      }
    ],
    "id":2
  }'
```
Response:
`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"state at block #127302882 is pruned"}}`

topIssues.title: flaky test: `XDM_MinGasLimits_Succeeds::invariant_minGasLimits`
topIssues.author: maurelian
topIssues.body:
https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/workflows/c9c37921-2268-4b12-a541-8034abfb303c (job `contracts-bedrock-tests-develop BRIDGE_HOOK`, [5757143](https://circleci.com/gh/ethereum-optimism/optimism/5757143))

Fails in about 1 in 6 `contracts-bedrock-tests-develop` jobs since #23619, which builds the contracts once and shares `cache/`, `artifacts/` and `forge-artifacts/` with the test jobs through the workspace. It did not fail before that change. It does not reproduce locally, and rerunning with the same `FOUNDRY_FUZZ_SEED` passes.

Every failure is a `relay` call with `value=1` that reverts with empty data ([`CrossDomainMessenger.t.sol#L84`](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/bb389124e2da8aa1ddce029e29c3ca01bb40317a/packages/contracts-bedrock/test/invariants/CrossDomainMessenger.t.sol#L84)). Diagnostics on #23638 show the cause. When the relay reverts, the portal and `0x04` both have balance 0, although `setUp` deals the portal `type(uint128).max` ([L108](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/bb389124e2da8aa1ddce029e29c3ca01bb40317a/packages/contracts-bedrock/test/invariants/CrossDomainMessenger.t.sol#L108)) and 1 to 7 earlier value relays in the same run succeeded:

```
DIAG value=1 data=0x opBalance=0 idBalance=0 valueRelays=2
```

The balances drop to zero mid-run, but code and storage survive. That points to forge (1.8.3-dev) rather than the contracts.

A/B test on #23638:

| Arm | Failures |
|---|---|
| Shared build, default invariant workers | 5 of 24 |
| Shared build, `FOUNDRY_INVARIANT_WORKERS=1` | 1 of 6 |
| Compile in the test job (as before #23619) | 0 of 18 |

🤖 *Co-created with Claude Opus 5.5*

topPRs.title: kona-node,kona-engine!: execute engine commands through one owner
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
An unsafe backlog or execution RPC failure can trap reset control, and derivation currently has to infer success from engine callbacks. Give execution mutations and resets one owner with bounded admission, epoch checks, acknowledged outcomes and state publication before replies. This removes the task heap, forwarding operation clients and callback state machine while keeping the independent kona-node connected to an external execution client.

Derived rejection now uses the L1 inclusion timestamp, distinguishes INVALID from temporary statuses, and performs the deposits-only replacement only where required. Pending span progress stays separate from completed safe/finalized progress; finality records carry the actual accepted block hash and inclusion source. Sequencer retries retain the retrieved payload, and full engine admission leaves networking responsive.

Stacked on #23488. The tracked [implementation plan](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/blob/codex/kona-refactor-05-engine-owner/docs/ai/kona-node-pr-plan.md) records scope and the remaining stack. Read-only RPC and sequencer-admin forwarding remain for their planned follow-ups; bootstrap policy and the canonical reset walk are preserved. The force-inclusion verifier receives one real startup block, then derives through the outage without L2 peers or further unsafe injection; idle-start bootstrap remains PR10.

Closes #22681. Its forced-inclusion regression is preserved by #23494 without a verifier startup payload primer; #23495 validates the recovered safe/finalized chain with engine-owned finality.

BREAKING CHANGE: replaces public Engine/task/error-severity wrappers and operation forwarding clients with ordinary kona-engine operations and kona-node-service EngineHandle. Downstream composition constructs EngineActor together with its handle; derived imports use ImportMode, EngineState includes phase/epoch/pending-safe, and producers carry captured context instead of sending raw operation messages.

Local validation: 321 offline tests, 115 focused tests, full workspace Rust lint, full repository Go lint, and a fresh default node build pass. The real short-window force-inclusion regression passes with a Kona sequencer and isolated Kona verifier. Four existing reorg subcases across both presets and both Kona restart tests also pass. Independent Rust/protocol, Go and deletion/API reviews completed; all actionable findings were fixed.

topPRs.title: kona-node!: start conductor-managed sequencers stopped
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
Conductor-managed Kona sequencers can become active on process startup without coordinated activation when `--sequencer.stopped` is omitted. They now always start stopped and wait for an explicit start, including when constructed directly through Rust.

Tenth PR in the stack, based on #23627. Preserves the remaining startup protection from #23578; #23581 and #23223 already supply its leadership checks and disaster-recovery behavior. Review against the immediate parent.

BREAKING CHANGE: Operators configuring `--conductor.rpc` must activate through conductor coordination, or explicitly call `admin_overrideLeader` followed by `admin_startSequencer` during disaster recovery. Leaving `--sequencer.stopped` unset no longer starts a conductor-managed sequencer automatically.

Validation: all 316 tests across kona-node-service, kona-node, and lokahi pass with all features and zero skips. Full workspace Rust lint passes, including formatting, Clippy, nightly documentation, and upstream-mirror checks. Independent Rust and startup/API reviews have no outstanding findings. Full devnet acceptance tests were not rerun locally.

topPRs.title: op-deployer,op-chain-ops!: run every deploy script on forge and delete the Go script host
topPRs.author: nonsense
topPRs.body:
This PR is split into a stack for review: #23663 → #23664 → #23665 → #23666 → #23667 → #23668 → #23669. The stack has later review fixes; this PR stays open as the CI-green reference.

op-deployer ran its deploy scripts on `op-chain-ops/script`, an in-process Go EVM. That host needs EVM hooks that only op-geth has (cheatcode precompiles, pranks, no code-size limit), so it blocks the move to upstream go-ethereum (#20266). After this PR, forge is the only script engine, and the Go host and `op-chain-ops/interopgen` are deleted.

**Effect on users**

- op-deployer runs forge for every deployment, and anvil for `prepare` and `continue`. It downloads the pinned Foundry release on Linux and macOS when the tools are not on PATH. The Docker images ship both.
- Genesis deployments (`apply --deployment-target genesis`, op-e2e, sysgo) run the scripts offline on forge. The L1 and L2 genesis output does not change: before the switch, a differential test found equal state roots from both engines on eight reference intents.
- Live `apply` and `bootstrap` broadcast with forge, one transaction at a time, and no longer through op-service's txmgr. As txmgr did, each transaction gets the node's gas estimate just before forge sends it, a tip of at least 1 gwei, and a fee cap of twice the base fee (at least 1 gwei) plus the tip. Unlike txmgr, forge does not bump the fee of, or resubmit, a stuck transaction. forge gets the deployer key in a temporary encrypted keystore that only the user can read, never on its command line.
- `prepare` and `continue` simulate the deployment on an ephemeral anvil fork of the L1, as the deployer, without its key. `continue` then checks the simulated transactions and replays them to L1 through txmgr.
- op-deployer never compiles. It refuses a contracts bundle that would make forge compile, or whose scripts have no `runWithBytes` entrypoint, and it stops forge as soon as forge starts to compile. So a bundle must come from the contracts release of the same op-deployer release: an `https://` or `file://` bundle of an earlier release is refused (`tag://` locators were already rejected). The default, `embedded`, works.
- A contracts bundle is a forge project, so op-deployer does not trust its `foundry.toml`: scripts run without the FFI cheatcode, with file access only to the artifacts and to op-deployer's state directory, and forge scripts and anvil inherit only the environment variables that they need (`verify-contract` keeps the full environment, for its API key). anvil listens on loopback without CORS.
- forge runs need the `lib/` sources of the bundle but no solc compiler. Each forge script loads every artifact of the project, about 1.3 GB, so forge runs take one of `GOMAXPROCS/2` slots per host.
- forge's output goes to stderr. A failed script reports its revert reason.
- Removed: the `calldata` and `noop` deployment targets, `op-deployer manage`, the `--use-forge` and `--forge-slow-broadcast` flags, the Windows release binaries and `DeploymentCalldata` in `state.json`. contracts-bedrock loses the `InteropMigration` script and `DummyCaller`.

**Reasons the diff does not show**

- Every forge run uses its own copy of the compile cache and its own broadcast directory, so that concurrent runs (devstack) do not interfere.
- Each broadcast sends one transaction at a time. Without `--slow`, forge waited forever when a node dropped one of several transactions that it sent at once.
- Bundle builds run one `forge script` to warm the script cache, as CI's `forge-build` already does. A single script's compile can choose other solc versions than the project build, and then forge compiles on the first run. The builds then check that a second run compiles nothing, and fail if it does.
- The interop harness and sysgo now run the interop migration on a live L1 through an EIP-7702 delegation from the ProxyAdmin owner, not in the genesis state. The L1 activates Prague at genesis for this.
- The test `RetryProxy` (op-service) now gives a client error (4xx, but not 429) to the client at once. forge calls methods such as `anvil_nodeInfo` that a proxyd endpoint answers with 403, and the proxy held each of these calls for about 40 s of retries, so the Sepolia tests of `init` timed out.
- sysgo waits for the L1 transaction index before it deploys: geth rejects receipt queries until its first indexing pass is done, and forge stops after a few quick retries.
- #23309 (genesis-output changes) is not in this PR, on purpose. It changes genesis output, which this PR must not do.
- CI jobs that run op-deployer from the checkout (op-e2e, sysgo, kona proof tests) now check out the contracts `lib/` submodules: forge reads the sources to check its compile cache, where the Go host read only artifact JSON.
- forge runs are not `--offline`: offline, forge requires every solc version of the cache installed even when it compiles nothing. Online, it resolves them from its built-in list and runs the cached artifacts.
- The `forge` package tests (anvil fork, compile stop, sandbox, environment, slots) run in CI only after #23643, which removes the package from the CI exclusion list.

**Review findings not fixed here**

- Live `apply`/`bootstrap` could keep txmgr by simulating on an anvil fork and replaying, as `continue` does. The #23300 plan chose `forge script --broadcast` for live deploys; this is a follow-up if fee bumping matters for these one-time deployments.
- The op-e2e interop harness and sysgo could share one `opcm.MigrateInput` type, and sysgo could check that its rollup configs and dependency set name the same chains, as interopgen did. Both are follow-ups.
- `opcm.NewForgeClient` takes no context for the forge download, and `opcm.PermissionedGameStartingAnchorRoot` now has only test users. Both are unchanged.
- Security review, not fixed: `continue` checks the sender, target, type and value of the call it replays, but not its calldata against the prepared input (that needs the script's encoding in Go); the RPC URL stays on the command line of forge and anvil, which have no environment binding for it; a crash during a broadcast can leave the encrypted keystore and its password file in a directory that only the user can read (forge refuses a password pipe); and a forge binary in the cache directory is trusted by its version.

Closes #23300, #23301, #23302, #23304, #23305, #23306, #23307 and #23308.

BREAKING CHANGE: The Go packages `op-chain-ops/script`, `op-chain-ops/interopgen`, `op-deployer/pkg/env`, `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/manage` and `op-deployer/pkg/deployer/upgrade` are removed. So are `opcm.Scripts`, the script-host `opcm` constructors, the `opcm.*ViaForge` functions (now `opcm.DeploySuperchain`, `opcm.DeployImplementations`, `opcm.DeployOPChain`, `opcm.DeployAltDA`, `opcm.DeployDisputeGame`, `opcm.DeployMIPS`, `opcm.DeployAlphabetVM`, `opcm.ReadImplementationAddresses` and `opcm.ReadSuperchainDeployment`, which take an `opcm.ForgeEnv`), `ApplyPipelineOpts.PrivateKey`, `UseForge` and `ReceiptQueryInterval`, and in `broadcaster` the `Broadcaster` interface, `CalldataBroadcaster`, `CaptureBroadcaster`, `NoopBroadcaster` and `BroadcastCreate2`. Go programs run Solidity scripts with forge, for example through op-deployer's `forge` package, take the upgrade input types from `opcm`, and build interop test worlds with an op-deployer intent. op-deployer users get forge and anvil from the release images, or let op-deployer download them. Users of `--use-forge`, `--forge-slow-broadcast`, or the `calldata` and `noop` targets drop them; forge is always used. Intents that point at an `https://` or `file://` bundle of an earlier contracts release use `embedded` instead. To move chains to interop, call `OPContractsManagerV2.migrate` as a delegatecall from the chains' ProxyAdmin owner, for example from a superchain-ops task.

topPRs.title: contracts-bedrock,op-core,op-interop-filter,kona!: per-message interop expiry and SuperchainETHBridge refunds
topPRs.author: karlfloersch
topPRs.body:
## Summary

Interop executing messages can't be forced in through deposits, so a destination sequencer that refuses to relay a message can keep it from ever being delivered. For `SuperchainETHBridge.sendETH`, that strands the ETH: it is burned on the source chain and never minted on the destination.

This PR lets the source chain learn, through censorship-resistant paths only, that a message can never be delivered. It exposes that per message as `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.expiredMessages(messageHash)`. `SuperchainETHBridge.refundETH` uses it to give the ETH back.

It replaces #22601, rebuilt on current `develop`. There is no registry, no admin setter, no app callback and no configurable window.

BREAKING CHANGE: `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.resendMessage` is removed, and the messenger now rejects messages whose target is the `L2CrossDomainMessenger` or the `L2ToL1MessagePasser` (`MessageTargetUnsafe`).
- **Who is affected:** applications and relayers that resend unrelayed interop messages, and anyone sending cross-chain messages to those two targets.
- **What breaks:** a message that isn't relayed within the expiry window can no longer be revived.
- **Configuration:** op-core and kona now refuse to load a dependency set whose `overrideMessageExpiryWindow` exceeds 604800 seconds (7 days), and `op-interop-filter` refuses `--message-expiry-window` above 168h. Operators with a longer override must lower it.
- **Migration:** treat an unrelayed message as expired, and undo the send on the source chain after `expiredMessages(messageHash)` is set, as `SuperchainETHBridge.refundETH` does. To reach L1 or the L2 messenger from a relayed message, go through your own contract.

## The protocol fact it builds on

An executing message is invalid when its block is more than the message expiry window (7 days) after its initiating message's block. Both cross-safety (op-supernode) and the fault proof (kona) enforce this, comparing the same two timestamps.

So once a destination's clock passes `sendTime + window` and the message is still unrelayed, no valid block can relay it. This PR carries that fact back to the source chain over a withdrawal followed by a deposit.

## How it works

For a message `H` sent from A to B and never relayed on B:

1. **On A, at send time:** `sendMessage` stores `sentMessageTimestamps[H] = block.timestamp`.
2. **On B, export:** anyone calls `UndeliveredMessageExporter.exportUndeliveredMessage(sourceMessenger, source, nonce, sender, target, message, minGasLimit)`. This is a new predeploy at `0x…0030`.
   - It hashes the message with **B's own chain ID as the destination**, so a chain can only speak for messages addressed to it.
   - It requires `!L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger.successfulMessages(H)`.
   - It sends `relayUndeliveredMessage(H, block.timestamp)` to `sourceMessenger`, which is A's `L1CrossDomainMessenger`, through the `L2CrossDomainMessenger`.
   - This is not an executing message, so if B censors it, it can be forced in as a deposit. The acceptance test does exactly that.
3. **On L1:** B's `L1CrossDomainMessenger` relays the withdrawal into A's `L1CrossDomainMessenger.relayUndeliveredMessage`. The function first requires that A has the `INTEROP` feature enabled. It then accepts the call only if:
   - the caller is a real `L1CrossDomainMessenger`: its portal's `SystemConfig` names it as that chain's messenger;
   - the caller's portal is authorized by **A's `ETHLockbox`**, meaning it is in A's cluster;
   - the L2 sender of the withdrawal is the **`UndeliveredMessageExporter`**.

   It then sends `expireMessage(H, undeliveredAt)` to A's `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger` as a deposit.
4. **On A, expire:** `expireMessage` accepts only the `L2CrossDomainMessenger` relaying from A's own `L1CrossDomainMessenger`, which is `otherMessenger()`, so L2 needs no new address. If `undeliveredAt > sentMessageTimestamps[H] + EXPIRY_PERIOD`, it sets `expiredMessages[H] = true`.
5. **On A, refund:** anyone calls `SuperchainETHBridge.refundETH(destination, nonce, from, to, amount)`. It rebuilds `H` from those arguments, requires `expiredMessages[H]`, and refunds `from` exactly once with a forced send.

**Why a refund can't double-spend:** B attests that H was unrelayed at a time past the window, and from then on the protocol rejects any relay of H. A acts only on a fact dated past `EXPIRY_PERIOD`, measured from a send time that is written once and never changes.

### Why the trusted sender is a new predeploy

The L1 side trusts withdrawals from the `UndeliveredMessageExporter` at `0x…0030`. It does not trust the `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger`.
- **No forged withdrawal can predate the upgrade.** The proxy at `0x…0030` had no implementation until this upgrade, so no withdrawal from it exists from before.
- **It can't be impersonated.** The exporter makes exactly one kind of call, so nothing can make it say something it didn't check.

The messenger, by contrast, has a history of relaying messages to arbitrary targets. Trusting it would let forged withdrawals created before the upgrade wait in unfinalized withdrawals or failed messages and be replayed afterwards. It would also open a window during any L1-before-L2 rollout.

### What prevents each attack
- **Forged facts from other chains:** every chain whose portal A's lockbox authorizes can already withdraw A's ETH, so trusting its facts adds no trust.
- **A forged messenger borrowing a real portal:** it fails the reverse binding.
- **Governance of another cluster chain:** that chain's governance could upgrade its own exporter and forge facts about any destination. That is the same trust as the shared `ETHLockbox` already places in it, since lockbox portals must share one proxy admin owner.
- **Something else sending the deposit as A's L1 messenger:** `L1CrossDomainMessenger` already refuses to relay messages that target itself, so only `relayUndeliveredMessage` can make it the sender.
- **The L1 call runs out of gas:** it lands in the calling messenger's failed messages, and anyone can replay it.
- **The wrong source messenger is named:** the deposit reverts on a chain that never sent `H`, and anyone can export again.
- **A fact that arrives too early:** it fails on A with `MessageNotExpired`. It can never succeed later, because its timestamp is fixed.

## Behavior changes (please review these closely)

- **`resendMessage` is removed** (`L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger` 2.0.0).
  - **Why:** resending lets a message be relayed for another window, which conflicts with expiry: a sender could resend, take a refund, and then have the resent event relayed. And letting anyone resend would let anyone stop a message from ever expiring.
  - **What happens instead:** an unrelayed message expires, and the app undoes the send.
  - **Who loses out:** apps without a refund, such as `SuperchainTokenBridge` today, lose the ability to revive an unrelayed message until they add one. See follow-ups.
- **The messenger refuses unsafe targets.** It won't send or relay messages whose target is the `L2CrossDomainMessenger` or the `L2ToL1MessagePasser` (`MessageTargetUnsafe`).
  - **This is defense in depth:** expiry's safety doesn't depend on it.
  - **What it guarantees:** the messenger never starts a withdrawal. Nothing that trusts it as a withdrawal sender, today or in future L1 contracts, can be fooled by a relayed message.
- **The expiry window can't exceed 7 days.** op-core and kona both reject a dependency-set message expiry window override above 7 days, and `op-interop-filter` caps its `--message-expiry-window` flag the same way. A window longer than the contract's period would allow a refund followed by a valid relay.
- **`EXPIRY_PERIOD = 8 days`:** the protocol's 7-day window plus a 1-day safety margin.
- **Every message costs more gas:** `sendMessage` stores a timestamp, about 22k more gas per message.
- **Old messages can't expire:** messages sent before this upgrade have no timestamp.

## Contract changes

- **`L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger` 1.3.2 → 2.0.0:**
  - new constant `EXPIRY_PERIOD`;
  - new storage at slots 3–4: `sentMessageTimestamps` and `expiredMessages`;
  - new function `expireMessage`, the unsafe-target helper, and `resendMessage` removed;
  - no initializer, so it is still upgraded with plain `upgradeTo`.
- **New `UndeliveredMessageExporter` 1.0.0 at `0x…0030`:** gated on interop like the other interop predeploys, and wired through `Predeploys`, `L2Genesis`, `L2ContractsManager` (now 1.15.0), the Go predeploy registry and the NUT bundle.
- **`L1CrossDomainMessenger` 2.11.1 → 2.12.0:** adds `relayUndeliveredMessage`, with no new storage and an `INTEROP` gate. `EXPIRE_MESSAGE_GAS_LIMIT = 100_000`, which a cold-storage relay test exercises.
- **`SuperchainETHBridge` 1.0.1 → 1.1.0:** `sendETH` is unchanged. Adds `refundETH` and a `refunded` mapping.
- **Off-chain:** the window cap in op-core (Go), kona (Rust) and `op-interop-filter`.
- **Docs:** `message-expiration.mdx` and the interop overview now describe expiry instead of resend.

## Launch checklist

- **The window cap is live before expiry is relied on.** Every node and the accepted proof program must enforce the dependency-set window cap of 7 days or less. With an older prestate that accepts a longer override, a refund could be followed by a valid relay.
- **The dependency set and the lockbox agree.** Every chain in a cluster's dependency set must also be authorized in the cluster's `ETHLockbox` and run the exporter, in the same fork. Otherwise sends to it can't be refunded.
- **Embed each cluster's dependency set in the prestate.** It must be in the registry and the absolute prestate: kona falls back to a host-supplied dependency set for clusters that aren't in the registry.
- **Re-snapshot Lagoon after merge.** Lagoon's NUT bundle (`op-core/nuts/fork_lock.toml`) still locks the old messenger. It must be re-snapshotted once this merges, together with kona's bundle counts, and the exporter added back to op-core's `Predeploys` map at that snapshot. It is deliberately left out until then, so the frozen fork state stays unchanged.
- **Rules every future upgrade must keep:**
  - nothing may re-emit `SentMessage` for a message that already has a timestamp: no resend, and no rollback to an implementation that has `resendMessage`;
  - every way of relaying on the destination must set `successfulMessages`;
  - any change to message hashing or nonce versioning must be mirrored in the exporter.

  Breaking any of these allows a refund followed by a relay.
- **Use enough L1 gas when finalizing an export,** at least 1M. Because a failed relay is stored rather than reverted, `eth_estimateGas` under-estimates.

## Limitations

- **Messages sent before the upgrade can't be recovered.** They have no send timestamp, so they can never expire, and with `resendMessage` gone they can't be resent either. In production this ships with interop's launch, so no messages predate it.
- **`refundETH` always pays `from`,** which is `sendETH`'s `msg.sender`. A router that sent ETH on someone's behalf needs its own way to pass a refund on. If `sendETH` was itself called from a relayed interop message, `from` is the `L2ToL2CrossDomainMessenger`, and a refund would be stuck there.
- **An early export is harmless.** It fails on the source with `MessageNotExpired`. Export again after `EXPIRY_PERIOD`.

## Testing

- **Forge:**
  - messenger: send timestamps, the unsafe-target rule on send and on relay, `expireMessage` auth and the exact boundary, and `expireMessage` through a real `L2CrossDomainMessenger` relay with cold storage, including an out-of-gas run then a replay;
  - exporter: hashing, the delivered check, and an export forced in from a deposit;
  - `L1CrossDomainMessenger`: an integration test with real contracts; rejection of a forged messenger, another lockbox, the wrong L2 sender (including `0x…23`), interop disabled, and the chain's own messenger;
  - bridge: refund after expiry pays exactly once; a forged refund through a direct `sendMessage` reverts; wrong-preimage fuzzing;
  - one end-to-end test of send → export → L1 → expire → refund, using `vm.warp`.
- **Acceptance (`op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/expiry`, two-chain interop devnet):** every leg runs for real:
  - `sendETH` from A, never relayed on B;
  - an export **forced in as an L1 deposit** on B;
  - prove and finalize, then A's L1 messenger relays and the deposit lands on A.

  The devnet can't advance L2 time 8 days, so the test then asserts the exact `MessageNotExpired` rejection, the carried hash and the timestamp. Forge covers the expired path. The acceptance test also checks ordinary relays and that exporting a delivered message is refused.
- **Go and Rust:** tests for the window cap, and tests pinning the constants.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- A spec section.
- Refunds in `SuperchainTokenBridge`, using the same `expiredMessages` check.
- Formal models and proofs, in a stacked draft PR: Lean, Quint, Kontrol, Halmos and invariant fuzzing.

topPRs.title: kona-node,op-acceptance-tests: serve the safe head history and compare it with op-node
topPRs.author: einar-oplabs
topPRs.body:
Stacked on #23583, which records the safe head history; review that first. This PR makes the record usable and proves it against op-node.

A kona-node started with `--safedb.path` (or `KONA_NODE_SAFEDB_PATH`) opens an on-disk safe head database and serves the two RPCs that proofs tooling reads from a rollup node. `optimism_safeHeadAtL1Block` was a stub answering method-not-found, which op-node's rollup client happens to read as an empty database; `superroot_atTimestamp` did not exist. Both answer in op-node's wire shape and with op-node's error messages, because that client recognizes a not-found answer by its message. A kona-node without the flag behaves as before, except that the stub now reports the database as not enabled instead of the method as missing. Combining the flag with derivation delegation is refused at startup, since a delegated node derives nothing and would serve a stale record.

Two differences from op-node surfaced only once the two ran side by side, and both are fixed here. op-node records the L2 genesis as safe from L1 block zero whenever derivation resets to genesis, so it answers for every L1 block below the first derived record; kona-node now does the same. And the super root preimage's timestamp is a hex quantity on the wire where the rest of the response uses plain integers.

The new `safeheaddb_parity` acceptance package runs an op-node verifier and a kona-node verifier on one chain, both recording, and asserts that every safe head answer and every super-root answer agree in both directions, through steady derivation, an L1 reorg, a kona-node CL restart, and a CL plus EL restart. It also checks that both nodes refuse the query the same way without a database. Written first, the package failed against the previous kona-node for exactly the reasons above; it passes against this branch locally. The mixed devstack runtime gained a per-node safe head database switch for it. The EL-resync scenario from #23585 is not in the package yet: kona-node clears its history when it resumes above the recorded tip (follow-up on #23474) and the devstack cannot wipe an op-reth data dir between a stop and a start.

Depends on #23514 for `CurrentL1`: kona-node reports the L1 head there today, where op-node reports the derivation origin, and op-challenger and op-proposer read that field from both RPCs' responses to decide whether a node is in sync. #23514 fixes it through the L1 watcher state that both RPCs here read from, so they inherit it with no change. It also touches the derivation actor constructor that #23583 changes, so this stack rebases onto develop once #23514 merges.

The `kona-gossip` commit is a cherry-pick of #23586 and disappears once that merges; without it kona-node cannot start on a host whose resolver configuration lists a scoped IPv6 nameserver, which is why the suite could not run here at first.

Closes #23475, closes #23476, closes #23477, closes #23585. Part of #23474, tracked under #23473.

Reviews run: `safedb-reviewer`, `rust-code-reviewer`, `go-code-reviewer`. Applied everything except: the `CurrentL1` finding is deferred to #23514 as above; the `kona-rpc` tests keep using the real rocksdb database rather than a stub, as the derivation actor tests already do; the suggestion to point the kona-sp1 decoders at these wire types is a follow-up. Reviewers should know `kona-rpc`'s test build now needs libclang locally.
